A metallophone in the broad sense is an idiophone whose sounding body is metal bars, tubes, rods, bowls or plates, not metal strings; it is usually struck with a mallet, and can also sound by friction, a keyboard mechanism or other means. Its Hornbostel-Sachs classification is 111.222, in the metal-plate class of struck idiophones. It has a long history of use in Asia and is common in Balinese and Javanese gamelan ensembles; the Western glockenspiel and vibraphone belong here too. After the twentieth century the single row of metal bars over a resonator was widely used in school music, and also appears in Carl Orff's teaching work Schulwerk, Xenakis's Pléïades and the music of Harry Partch.
鐵琴的發聲體為金屬條、管、棒、碗或板，而非金屬弦；通常以琴槌敲擊，亦可經摩擦、鍵: The sounding body of a metallophone is metal bars, tubes, rods, bowls or plates rather than metal strings; it is usually struck with a mallet, and can also be set going by friction, a keyboard action or other means. The pitch depends on the instrument: gamelan uses a single row of metal bars tuned to the pélog or sléndro scale; the Western glockenspiel and vibraphone use two rows of bars, modelled on the piano keyboard and tuned chromatically; teaching instruments are often tuned diatonically, and some are tuned microtonally. The source does not mention a specific range or any means of controlling volume. What separates it from instruments of the same family is chiefly the metal sounding body, the number of rows and the tuning system.
鐵琴類樂器在亞洲音樂中已有數千年使用歷史，巴厘島與爪哇甘美蘭合奏中的 gendè: Metallophones have been used in Asian music for thousands of years; the gendèr, gangsa and saron of Balinese and Javanese gamelan are mostly single rows of metal bars, tuned to the pélog or sléndro scale. The Western glockenspiel and vibraphone have two rows of bars, modelled on the piano keyboard and tuned chromatically. Since the twentieth century the word metallophone has sometimes meant specifically a single row of metal bars suspended over a resonator; the diatonically tuned kind is common in schools, and Carl Orff used it in works such as Schulwerk, while microtonally tuned instruments appear in Iannis Xenakis's Pléïades and the music of Harry Partch.
